newsitem.title: USA: Intermet sees $186 million net merger cost.
newsitem.headline: Intermet sees $186 million net merger cost.

text.p: Intermet Corp said Tuesday it expects the net cost of its merger with Sudbury Inc to be $186 million, which it plans to finance with cash and new borrowings. Both companies are automotive suppliers.
It expects the merger to boost Intermet earnings in the first year by about $0.35 before expenses, Intermet chairman and chief executive officer John Doddridge said in a conference call.
The Detroit-based foundry firm said Monday Cleveland-based Sudbury agreed to Intermet's $12.50 a share cash tender offer for all outstanding shares of Sudbury.
The tender will begin as soon as possible, subject only to regulatory conditions, Doddridge said, adding Intermet expects to complete the merger in mid-January.

"We expect the merger to be accretive to Intermet shareholders, theoretically about $0.35 a share in year one but the actual (earnings) improvement will probably be less in the first year (due to merger-related expenses)," he said.
"Assuming the economy holds, we should experience even better accretive values in year two and year three," he said.
Doddridge said Intermet expects the purchase price to be about $195 million and transaction costs to be $5 million.

But he said Intermet will benefit by about $14 million when options and participation certifications on 4.2 million Sudbury shares are exercised, bringing net cost to $186 million. Total share outstanding (diluted) are 15.6 million.
The cost will be financed with $35 million Intermet cash, $2 million Sudbury cash and $149 million in new Intermet borrowings, Doddridge said.

Sudbury has five units, including a powder coatings unit and a truck body and crane unit that will be new businesses for Intermet, Doddridge said. But Intermet has no plans to divest any of the units, which are all profitable, he said.
Sudbury's Wagner Castings, Frisby precision machined components and Cast-Matic die castings unit mesh with Intermet's core ferrous casting foundry business, he said.
He also said Intermet will retain most or possibly all Sudbury employees except chairman and chief executive officer Jacques Sardas, 65, who plans to retire.
Sardas took the Sudbury helm in 1992 while the company was in Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Doddridge credited Sardas with building a growing, profitable company with "almost no debt."
Doddridge also said Intermet continues to seek additional foundry capacity in Europe.
